title: Scaling Physical Reasoning with the PHYSICS Dataset
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of high-quality physics data and physics-specific evaluation methods for large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that physics reasoning is important, but existing benchmarks are limited in scale, difficulty coverage, language coverage, and evaluation robustness, especially for issues such as unit conversion and numerical simplification.

To address this, they introduce PHYSICS, a bilingual English-Chinese dataset of 16,568 physics questions derived from over 100 textbooks and exercise books. The dataset spans five domains: Mechanics, Electromagnetism, Thermodynamics, Optics, and Modern Physics, and covers difficulty levels from high school to graduate-level physics. The dataset is split into training and test sets, and the training portion includes reasoning paths generated by strong reasoning models. The paper also proposes a Rule+Model hybrid evaluation framework, combining rule-based verification with a fine-tuned model verifier specialized for physics answers.

The paper evaluates many open-source and proprietary LLMs on the PHYSICS test set and finds that even strong models struggle with physics reasoning relative to their math performance. Reasoning models outperform chat models, open-source models are closing the gap but still lag behind closed-source models overall, and performance varies across physics domains, difficulty levels, and languages. Fine-tuning on the PHYSICS training data improves performance on physics benchmarks and also yields some gains on math and general reasoning benchmarks.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/dataset construction and model evaluation paper, not a K-12 intervention study or controlled educational trial. It provides useful empirical evidence on physics reasoning benchmarks, but the methodology is primarily benchmark-based rather than experimental with learners.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear performance gains for LLMs on physics reasoning tasks, but these are model-benchmark improvements rather than demonstrated learner outcomes. Its educational impact on K-12 is indirect and currently unclear.

interventions.use_case: Construction of a large physics problem dataset for LLM training and evaluation, plus a physics-specific hybrid Rule+Model answer verification framework (rule-based unit/simplification checks followed by a fine-tuned judge model).

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that fine-tuning on the PHYSICS training set improves physics reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks. For example, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct improved from 22.30% to 32.85% on PHYSICS (+10.55 points), and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct improved from 27.65% to 40.20% (+12.55 points). Similar gains were seen on GPQA (Physics), OlympiadBench (Physics), and UGPhysics, indicating stronger scientific/physics reasoning after training.
finding.measure: Accuracy on PHYSICS test set, GPQA (Physics), OlympiadBench (Physics), and UGPhysics
